edition.locus: Bd I 3 (ch. I, opening Isaiah epigraph and address)

pass_a_gloss: Those weaned off milk, those pulled away from the breast: receive tribulation on tribulation, receive hope on hope, still a little, still a little, on account of contempt of lips, through a different tongue. And you then, according to Isaiah, as no longer fleshly nor infants in Christ, having made progress in your intelligible age, most God-revering Ambrose and most pious Protoctetus, and no longer having need of milk but of solid nourishment, hear, as weaned off milk and pulled from the breast, in what manner to the weaned, as to athletes, not a single tribulation but a certain tribulation on tribulation is prophesied. The one not pushing off the tribulation on tribulation but receiving it as a well-born athlete straightaway receives also hope on hope, which he will enjoy not much after the tribulation on tribulation; for of this kind is the 'still a little, still a little'.
pass_b_english: “You who are weaned from milk, you who are drawn from the breast, welcome affliction upon affliction, welcome hope upon hope; yet a little, yet a little, because of the scorn of lips, by another tongue” (Isaiah 28:9-11).

You too, then, most God-fearing Ambrose and most devout Protoctetus, are in Isaiah's sense no longer people of the flesh, nor babes “in Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:1); you have advanced “in” the inward “stature” of your minds (Luke 2:52), and you no longer “need milk” but “solid food” (Hebrews 5:12). So listen, as those “weaned from milk” and “drawn from the breast”, to how, for the weaned, as for athletes, what is prophesied is not a simple affliction but a kind of “affliction upon affliction”. Whoever does not thrust away the affliction “upon affliction”, but welcomes it like a noble athlete, at once welcomes “hope upon hope” as well, and he will enjoy that hope not long after the affliction “upon affliction”. For that is what “yet a little, yet a little” means.

choices.choice: 2026-11-11: retranslated in full from Koetschau (GCS 2, ch. I, opening); the old English was a digest; it kept the outline but ran clauses together, left Isaiah's lines in a stiff word-for-word order and piled the references at the end instead of at the quotations.
“in Isaiah's sense”: Origen applies Isaiah's “weaned” to the addressees, so the phrase governs the whole description of them.
“the inward stature of your minds”: νοητός is the intelligible, inner stature, set against the bodily stature of Luke 2:52.
Read ἀπογεγαλακτισμένοι, οὐκέτι, σάρκινοι, προκόψαντες, μηκέτι, Πρωτόκτητε, θλῖψις ἐπὶ θλίψει (OCR 'Hiper'), ἔτι μικρόν (OCR ἔτε).

source_text: „Oi ἀπογεγαλακτισμένοε ἀπὸ γάλακτος, οἱ ἀπεσπασμένοι ἀπὸ μαστοῦ, ϑλῖψιν ἐπὶ ϑλίψει προσδέχου, προσδέχου ἐλπίδα ἐπ᾽ ἐλπίδι, ἔτι μικρὸν ἔτι μικρὸν, διὰ φαυλισμὸν χειλέων, διὰ γλώσσης ἑτέρας." καὶ ὑμεῖς τοίνυν κατὰ τὸν Ἡσαΐαν ὡς οὐχέτε σάρχινοι οὐδὲ (ἐν Χριστῷ" νήπιοι προχόψαντες „ev τῇ“ νοητῇ ὑμῶν ,ἡλικίᾳ", ᾿Αμβρόσιε ϑεοσεβέστατε καὶ Πρωτόχτητε εὐσεβέστατε, καὶ μηκέτε (χρείαν ἔχοντες γάλακτος" ἀλλὰ" ,στερεᾶς τροφῆς", ἀκούετε ὡς ,ἀπογεγαλακτισμένοι ἀπὸ γάλακτος" καὶ ,ἀπεσπασμένοι ἀπὸ μαστοῦ", τίνα τρόπον ὡς ἀϑληταῖς τοῖς ἀπογεγαλαχτισμένοις οὐχ ἁπλῆ ϑλῖψις ἀλλά τις »ϑλῖψις ἐπὶ Hiper“ προφητεύεται. ὁ δὲ μὴ ἀπωϑούμενος τὴν (ἐπὶ ϑλίψει:" ϑλῖψιν͵ ἀλλ᾽ ὡς γενναῖος ἀϑλητὴς αὐτὴν “προσδεχόμενος εὐϑέως προσδέχεται καὶ ,ἐλπίδα ἐπ’ ἐλπίδι", ἧς μετ᾽ οὐ πολὺ τῆς »ἐπὶ ϑλίψει" ϑλίψεως ἀπολαύσει' τοιοῦτο γάρ ἐστι τὸ ,͵ἔτε μικρὸν ἔτε μικρόν."
